meta.titre: Water Relations in Plant Cells: water potential and its pathways
meta.sous_theme: Water potential, turgor and pathways of water

sections.contenu_markdown: In the dry season in the Far North Region, tomato and cassava leaves wilt at midday and stand up again in the evening or after watering. The plant has not changed, only the water inside its cells. Plants have no muscles; they rely on water pressure inside their cells to stay upright, and water moves between cells according to a measurable quantity called water potential. GCE Advanced Level papers ask you to define water potential, to calculate its components, to predict the direction of water movement and to describe the pathways taken by water.

items: Osmosis is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane.
A plant cell has a cellulose cell wall outside the plasma membrane and a large central vacuole bounded by the tonoplast.
Plasmodesmata are narrow cytoplasmic channels that pass through the cell walls of neighbouring plant cells.

sections.titre: Water potential, turgor and the movement of water
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Water potential** ($\psi$) is a measure of the tendency of water molecules to move from one place to another. It is measured in **kilopascals (kPa)**. Pure water at standard temperature and atmospheric pressure has the highest value, $\psi = 0$. All solutions have a **negative** water potential, and the more concentrated the solution, the more negative the value. Water moves by osmosis **from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to a region of lower (more negative) water potential**, down the water potential gradient.

For a plant cell:

$$\psi_{\text{cell}} = \psi_s + \psi_p$$

- **Solute potential** ($\psi_s$) is the effect of dissolved solutes on water potential. It is always **zero or negative**, and more negative for more concentrated sap.
- **Pressure potential** ($\psi_p$) is the pressure exerted on the cell contents by the cell wall. It is usually **positive** in a turgid cell and zero in a flaccid cell.

| State of the cell | Pressure potential | Water potential |
|---|---|---|
| Fully turgid, at equilibrium with pure water | $\psi_p = -\psi_s$ (positive) | $0$ |
| Partly turgid | positive, smaller | negative |
| Flaccid, **incipient plasmolysis** | $0$ | $\psi_s$ |
| Plasmolysed (membrane pulled away from the wall) | $0$ | $\psi_s$ of the shrunken cell, more negative than before |

A **turgid** cell is full of water and pressed against its wall; turgor supports non-woody stems and leaves and opens stomata. **Plasmolysis** happens when a cell is placed in a solution with a lower water potential than the cell: water leaves, the vacuole shrinks and the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall.

At equilibrium between a cell and its surroundings the water potentials are equal. A cell placed in pure water or a dilute solution takes up water until $\psi_{\text{cell}}$ equals that of the solution; the wall then prevents the cell from bursting.

variantes.nom: Movement of water between neighbouring cells
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the water potentials of two or more cells are given and the direction of flow is asked.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Calculate $\psi$ of each cell from $\psi_s+\psi_p$. Water moves from the cell with the higher (less negative) $\psi$ to the cell with the lower (more negative) $\psi$. A series of cells with decreasing $\psi$ from the cortex towards the xylem keeps water flowing inward. Do not compare $\psi_s$ values alone, because the pressure potential matters too.

variantes.nom: Pathways of water across a root
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how water gets from the root hairs to the xylem.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The **apoplast pathway** runs through the cell walls and intercellular spaces, where water moves by mass flow and capillary action without crossing a membrane. The **symplast pathway** runs through the cytoplasm of cells connected by **plasmodesmata**; water entered the cytoplasm by osmosis across the plasma membrane. In the **vacuolar pathway** water passes from cell to cell through the vacuoles, crossing both the plasma membrane and the tonoplast (some books count it as part of the symplast route). Membrane crossing is helped by water channel proteins called **aquaporins**. At the endodermis the **Casparian strip**, a band of waterproof suberin in the walls, blocks the apoplast pathway, forcing water into the cytoplasm, so that the endodermis selects what enters the xylem.

sections.enonce_markdown: A mesophyll cell has a solute potential of $-1100$ kPa and a pressure potential of $+650$ kPa. It is placed in a large volume of solution of water potential $-800$ kPa. (Assume that the solute potential of the cell stays constant because its volume changes very little.) Calculate the water potential of the cell, state the direction of net water movement and calculate the pressure potential of the cell when it reaches equilibrium.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that the solute potential of a cell sap is positive.
items.pourquoi_faux: Dissolved solutes lower the water potential, so solute potential is zero for pure water and negative for any solution.
items.correction_markdown: Always write $\psi_s$ as a negative number, for example $-900$ kPa.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that water moves from a region of low water potential to a region of high water potential.
items.pourquoi_faux: Water moves down a gradient from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. Confusion arises from comparing the numbers without their signs.
items.correction_markdown: Remember that $-300$ kPa is higher than $-600$ kPa, so water moves from $-300$ to $-600$ kPa.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving the pressure potential of a plasmolysed or flaccid cell as a large positive number.
items.pourquoi_faux: A flaccid cell is not pressing against its wall, so its pressure potential is zero and $\psi_{\text{cell}}=\psi_s$.
items.correction_markdown: Take $\psi_p = 0$ at incipient plasmolysis and for plasmolysed cells.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that the water potential of pure water is $+100$ kPa or $1$ kPa.
items.pourquoi_faux: By definition the water potential of pure water at standard temperature and pressure is zero, the maximum value.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that all water moves through a root by osmosis across membranes.
items.pourquoi_faux: In the apoplast pathway, water moves through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing a membrane until it reaches the endodermis.
items.correction_markdown: Osmosis across membranes occurs in the symplast and vacuolar pathways and, because the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast, at the endodermis.

items.enonce_markdown: A leaf cell has a solute potential of $-700$ kPa and a pressure potential of $+500$ kPa. Calculate its water potential.

Cell A has a water potential of $-400$ kPa and the neighbouring cell B has a water potential of $-650$ kPa. (a) State the direction of net water movement between them and the size of the gradient. (b) Cell C has a solute potential of $-950$ kPa. It is left in pure water until equilibrium. Calculate its water potential and pressure potential.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A has the higher water potential, so water moves **from A to B**. Gradient $= (-400) - (-650) =$ **250 kPa**.

(b) At equilibrium with pure water $\psi_{\text{cell}} =$ **0 kPa**. $\psi_p = \psi_{\text{cell}} - \psi_s = 0 - (-950) =$ **$+950$ kPa**.

items.enonce_markdown: Four cells P, Q, R and S in a root have water potentials of $-300$, $-450$, $-600$ and $-750$ kPa respectively. (a) State the direction in which water moves along the chain and the gradient between each pair of neighbours. (b) Cell Q has a solute potential of $-900$ kPa. Calculate its pressure potential. (c) Q is then placed in a large volume of solution of water potential $-300$ kPa. State what happens and calculate its pressure potential at equilibrium, assuming its solute potential stays constant. (d) Name the structure that stops water moving through the cell walls into the xylem.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Water moves from P to Q to R to S (high to low). Each gradient is $150$ kPa, for example $(-300) - (-450) = 150$ kPa.

(b) $\psi_p = \psi_{\text{cell}} - \psi_s = (-450) - (-900) =$ **$+450$ kPa**.

(c) The solution ($-300$ kPa) has a higher water potential than Q ($-450$ kPa), so water enters Q by osmosis and Q becomes more turgid. At equilibrium $\psi_{\text{cell}} = -300$ kPa and $\psi_p = (-300) - (-900) =$ **$+600$ kPa**.

(d) The **Casparian strip** in the endodermis, which blocks the apoplast pathway.

items_markdown: $\psi_{\text{cell}}=\psi_s+\psi_p$, measured in kPa; pure water has $\psi=0$ and solutions are negative.
Water moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential, and at equilibrium the potentials are equal.
A turgid cell has a positive $\psi_p$; a flaccid or plasmolysed cell has $\psi_p=0$ so $\psi=\psi_s$; in pure water at equilibrium $\psi_p=-\psi_s$.

Water crosses a root by the apoplast, symplast (cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata) and vacuolar (through vacuoles, crossing plasma membrane and tonoplast) pathways; the Casparian strip at the endodermis forces water through the cytoplasm.
Turgor supports non-woody parts, and loss of turgor causes wilting; plasmolysis is the shrinking of the protoplast away from the wall.
